notes:
Based on the sources I was able to access, here are verse-by-verse notes:

---

## 2 Kings 4:23–44 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 23: "Why would you go to him today? … It is not a New Moon or a Sabbath."

- **New Moon and Sabbath as teaching days:** The husband's objection reveals that in the Northern Kingdom, pious Israelites customarily visited prophets on new moons and Sabbaths for religious instruction and edification. Her visit on an ordinary day seemed unnecessary to him.
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **"Everything is all right" (shalom):** The woman answers with the single Hebrew word *shalom* ("peace"), used like "all right" in English, to satisfy her husband without disclosing the death. Gill notes she meant "be easy and quiet, farewell."
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html
  — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-4.html

- **The husband's unawareness:** He evidently had no idea the child was dead or even in danger. The Pulpit Commentary notes he probably "had not realized to himself that he was in any danger."
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html

---

### v. 24: "She saddled the donkey … Drive onward; do not slow the pace … unless I tell you."

- **Her urgency:** The Shunammite woman showed determined haste. The Pulpit Commentary notes Shunem to Carmel was at least 14–15 miles. She instructs the servant to keep a vigorous pace and not slacken unless she herself commands.
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **Faith in action:** Enduring Word notes this woman's faith was demonstrated by action — she prepared for resurrection, not burial.
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 25: "She set out and went to the man of God at Mount Carmel."

- **Carmel as Elisha's retreat:** Elisha dwelt at Carmel at least occasionally. It was to him what Gilead had been to Elijah — a place for solitary retirement, meditation, and communion with God. It served as a fixed centre of prophetic teaching for the north.
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **"Look, there is the Shunammite woman":** Elisha recognised her at a distance, probably by her attire and carriage. The Pulpit Commentary suggests she was among those accustomed to attend gatherings on new moons and Sabbaths.
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html

---

### v. 26: "Run out now to meet her … 'Are you all right? … your husband … your child?'"

- **Elisha's pastoral concern:** Elisha sensed something was wrong and sent Gehazi with three rapid, specific questions. Enduring Word cites Maclaren: "Nothing makes grief dumb so surely as prying and yet indifferent intrusion."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **She answered, "Everything is all right":** She gave the same ambiguous answer as to her husband. She would not pour out her grief to Gehazi; she wanted the prophet himself.
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
  — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-4.html

---

### v. 27: "She clung to his feet … her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me."

- **Clasping his feet:** This was the posture of an urgent, humble supplicant. It parallels Ruth 3:9. Gehazi thought it a trespass on his master's dignity and moved to push her away.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
  — BibleHub Q&A: https://biblehub.com/q/Elisha_s_insight_and_limits_in_2_Kings_4_27.htm

- **"The LORD has hidden it from me":** This is a key statement about prophetic limitation. Elisha openly acknowledges that supernatural knowledge is not intrinsic to him — it is given by God, and God may withhold it. The BibleHub article notes: "True prophecy operates only as God wills … The episode refutes any occultic or clairvoyant caricature." The Pulpit Commentary says Elisha was more surprised that God *didn't* speak than if He had.
  — BibleHub Q&A: https://biblehub.com/q/Elisha_s_insight_and_limits_in_2_Kings_4_27.htm
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html

- **Chuck Smith (Pentecostal/Calvary Chapel) notes on this verse:** Smith taught that God inserted this detail "lest people … attribute that to some kind of mental capacities, mind reading or whatever. God inserted this into the stories so that you would know that his was a gift of God and God could withhold that gift."
  — StudyLight.org / Chuck Smith commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/4-26.html

- **Maclaren (Reformed/Baptist):** "How much better would it have been for the Church if its teachers had been more willing to copy his modesty, and said about a great many things, 'The Lord hath hid it from me'!"
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 28: "Did I ask you for a son, my lord? Didn't I say, 'Do not deceive me'?"

- **Her complaint:** She is not accusing Elisha of deception but expressing the anguish of having a gift given and then torn away. Ellicott says: "Better to have had no son, than to have had one and lost him." The Pulpit Commentary notes her words echo her earlier incredulity (v.16). She is pleading: "You gave me the son — now restore him."
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html
  — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-4.html

---

### v. 29: "Tie up your garment, take my staff … do not greet him … lay my staff on the boy's face."

- **Girding the loins:** Tucking the long robe into the belt signalled readiness for rapid travel (cf. Exodus 12:11; 1 Kings 18:46). Elisha required immediate action.
  — BibleHub Q&A: https://biblehub.com/q/Elisha_s_staff_s_role_in_2_Kings_4_29.htm
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **No greetings:** Eastern greetings could be prolonged and elaborate. Elisha forbids all social distractions for the sake of urgent mission. Jesus gave identical instructions in Luke 10:4.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
  — BibleHub Q&A: https://biblehub.com/q/Lessons_on_Elisha_s_authority_to_Gehazi.htm

- **The staff:** It represented Elisha's prophetic authority, but was *not* a magical object. The BibleHub article states: "The staff alone does not raise the boy (v.31), reminding us that faith rests in the living God, not in objects." Ellicott notes two views: (a) if the mother had faith, the staff might have sufficed; (b) Keil (Lutheran) thinks Elisha foresaw the failure and intended it to teach that power resides in Jehovah alone, not in the prophet or his staff.
  — BibleHub Q&A: https://biblehub.com/q/Elisha_s_staff_s_role_in_2_Kings_4_29.htm
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

---

### v. 30: "As surely as the LORD lives … I will not leave you."

- **Her insistence:** The Shunammite had no faith in Gehazi or the staff alone. She refused to leave Elisha. Enduring Word suggests she may have "failed under this test" because she thought the power was more connected with Elisha himself and refused to leave his presence. Yet her persistence also reveals her faith that Elisha *could* help.
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
  — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-4.html

---

### v. 31: "Gehazi went on ahead … there was no sound or response."

- **The failure:** The staff produced no result. The child did not awaken. Ellicott notes that "The Rabbis explain Gehazi's failure by assuming that he had disobeyed his master's injunction by loitering on the way. This is contradicted by the narrative itself." Bähr (cited by Ellicott) thought Elisha himself was at fault for acting in "over-haste without a Divine incentive." But Ellicott favours the view that the failure was meant to teach that miracle-working power is not magically transferable.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 32: "When Elisha reached the house, there was the boy lying dead on his bed."

- **"His bed":** The child was on Elisha's own bed in the prophet's chamber — where the mother had laid him (v.21). This detail prepares for the intimate contact of the resurrection miracle.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 33: "He went in, closed the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the LORD."

- **Privacy and prayer:** Elisha followed his mentor Elijah's pattern (1 Kings 17:20-23). He shut the door — excluding all onlookers — and prayed. Enduring Word notes: "Elisha prayed with great faith because he knew God worked this way in the life of his mentor Elijah."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **Contrast with Christ:** Enduring Word highlights the significant contrast between Elisha's stretched-out, begging supplication and Jesus' authoritative command (John 11:43). "Elijah and Elisha rightly begged God to raise the dead. Jesus commanded the dead to be raised."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 34: "Elisha got on the bed and lay on the boy, mouth to mouth, eye to eye, hand to hand … the boy's body became warm."

- **The physical contact:** This is modelled on Elijah's raising of the widow's son (1 Kings 17:21), but described in greater detail. The life of the Divine Spirit in Elisha was "miraculously imparted by contact to the lifeless body."
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **Symbolic reading:** Maclaren (cited by Enduring Word) sees a profound typology: "If we regard it as symbolic of that closeness of approach to our nature, dead in sins, which the Lord of life makes in His incarnation and in His continual drawing near."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

- **Ceremonial uncleanness:** Matthew Poole (cited by Enduring Word) notes that touching a dead body brought ceremonial uncleanness, but this "was justly to give place to a moral duty, and to an action of so great piety and charity … especially when done by a prophet, and by the instinct of God's Spirit, who can dispense with his own laws."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 35: "Elisha … paced back and forth … stretched himself out … the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes."

- **A gradual miracle:** Unlike some instantaneous miracles, this one unfolded by degrees. Poole (cited by Enduring Word) notes: "Although miracles were for the most part done in an instant, yet sometimes they were done by degrees, as here, and 1 Kings 18:44-45; Mark 8:24-25."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

- **"Paced back and forth":** Ellicott says Elisha's walking "is an index of intense excitement. He was earnestly expecting the fulfilment of his prayer."
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **"Sneezed seven times":** The sneezing was a sign of restored respiration. The Hebrew verb occurs only here. Keil (Lutheran) argued that the gradual nature of the miracle compared to Elijah's instant one "betokens an inferiority on the part of Elisha," but Ellicott counters that the narrative in 1 Kings 17 is "plainly abridged."
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

---

### vv. 36–37: "Call the Shunammite woman … Pick up your son … she fell at his feet."

- **Elisha's pastoral touch:** He summoned the mother and simply said, "Pick up your son," paralleling Jesus' words in Luke 7:15: "He delivered him to his mother."
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **Her worship:** She fell at his feet and bowed to the ground in deep reverence — not worship of Elisha, but of the God whose power Elisha mediated.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

---

### v. 38: "When Elisha returned to Gilgal … famine in the land … sons of the prophets were sitting at his feet."

- **New episode:** This begins a separate narrative, not necessarily in chronological sequence with the preceding. "Sitting before him" means sitting as disciples before a master.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **The famine:** Enduring Word notes this may be the seven-year famine alluded to in 2 Kings 8:1-3. The "sons of the prophets" were a company of prophetic disciples living in community.
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

- **"Put on the large pot":** In a time of scarcity, Elisha showed practical care for the community by ordering stew to be prepared.
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 39: "One of them … found a wild vine … gathered wild gourds … cut them up into the pot."

- **The wild gourds:** These were probably *colocynth* (citrullus colocynthis), also called "wild cucumber." Dilday (cited by Enduring Word) notes: "When the gourds are cut open the pulp dries rapidly and forms a powder, which … is still used as a cathartic medicine. It has a very bitter taste. If eaten in enough quantity, it induces colic and can be fatal."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

- **"Though no one knew what they were":** The gatherer mistook the poisonous gourds for edible ones. Ellicott notes that edible gourds were "a favourite food of the people" (Numbers 11:5).
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

---

### v. 40: "There is death in the pot, O man of God!"

- **The cry of alarm:** The men recognised the poison as soon as they tasted it. Enduring Word notes that Elisha "felt a special responsibility to help in this situation because he told the men to gather ingredients for the stew."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

- **Spurgeon's application (Baptist):** "You have been trying to find pleasure in the world, and you have found wild vines … you have gathered wild gourds, a lap full, almost a heart full. You have been shredding death into the pot … If you are a child of God, you will cry out, 'O thou man of God, there is death in the pot!'"
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 41: "Get some flour … threw it into the pot … there was nothing harmful in the pot."

- **The flour:** There was nothing inherently purifying in the flour — the real purification was a miraculous work of God. The Pulpit Commentary says: "The 'meal' here … corresponds to the 'salt' in 2 Kings 2:21." Keil (Lutheran, cited by Ellicott) says the meal "was only the material basis for the spiritual activity which went out from Elisha, and made the poisonous food wholesome."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **Spurgeon's ecclesiological application (Baptist):** "I believe it is to imitate Elisha. We need not attempt to get the wild gourds out of the pot; they are cut too small … We must look to God for help … 'Bring meal.' Good wholesome food was cast into the poisonous stuff, and by God's gracious working it killed the poison; and the Church must cast the blessed gospel of the grace of God into the poisoned pottage."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 42: "A man from Baal-shalishah came … with twenty loaves of barley bread from the first ripe grain."

- **Firstfruits offering:** According to Numbers 18:13 and Deuteronomy 18:4, firstfruits were normally reserved for God and for the Levitical priests. Patterson and Austel (cited by Enduring Word) note that "because the religion in the Northern Kingdom was apostate, the loaves had been brought … to the one whom he considered to be the true repository of godly religion in Israel."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **Baal-shalishah:** Identified by Jerome and Eusebius as about 15 Roman miles north of Lydda-Diospolis, west of Gilgal. Its name ("Three-land") may refer to three wadies meeting there.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **Peake's Commentary** notes that in the early Christian *Didache* (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), "the prophets are to be given of the firstfruits, 'for they are your priests.' There is no similar instance in the OT" — making this passage a rare OT precedent for firstfruits being given to a prophet rather than a priest.
  — Peake's Commentary (StudyLight): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-kings-4.html

---

### v. 43: "How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men? … 'They will eat and have some left over.'"

- **The servant's objection:** The servant saw only natural insufficiency. The Pulpit Commentary notes the servant "felt that the quantity was quite insufficient, and thought it absurd to invite a hundred men."
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **"Thus says the LORD":** Elisha did not perform this miracle himself — he only predicted it. Keil (Lutheran, cited by Ellicott) calls attention to the fact that "Elisha does not perform, but only predicts, this miracle." This is a promise from God, not a prophetic incantation.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "What can these few cakes do towards feeding a hundred men? They forget that God can multiply them. Ye limit the Holy One of Israel. Do you think he needs our numbers? … I tell you, our weakness is a better weapon for God than our strength."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

---

### v. 44: "They ate and had some left over, according to the word of the LORD."

- **A type of Christ's feeding miracles:** This miracle clearly anticipates Jesus' feeding of the 5,000 and 4,000. Clarke (cited by Enduring Word) says: "This is something like our Lord's feeding the multitude miraculously. Indeed, there are many things in this chapter similar to facts in our Lord's history; and this prophet might be more aptly considered a type of our Lord, than most of the other persons in the Scripture who have been thus honored."
  — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

- **Debate about the nature of the miracle:** Bähr (cited by Ellicott and Pulpit Commentary) denied any miraculous increase, arguing the hundred men were merely satisfied with their small portions. Thenius thought the provisions were adequate for a hundred men. But both Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary reject this: "This is certainly opposed to the sacred writer's intention." Keil (Lutheran) says it was a genuine miracle of multiplication, analogous to Christ's feedings.
  — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
  — Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-4.html

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist):** Notes the connection to the disciples at the miracle of the loaves and fishes, but adds "that must be allowed to be a greater miracle than this" (Matthew 14:17), since Jesus fed far more with far less.
  — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-4.html

---

## Denominational Perspectives

The sources I could access did not yield extensive separate treatments by denomination for this passage. However, the following distinctions emerged:

- **Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):** Strong emphasis on the sovereignty of God in the miracles, the non-magical nature of the prophetic office, the typological reading of the stew as the church needing pure gospel (flour) to overcome worldly poison, and the primacy of faith. Spurgeon especially uses the "death in the pot" as a vivid warning against worldliness in the church.

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (David Guzik / Enduring Word, Chuck Smith):** Emphasis on faith as cooperation with God's miracle-working power. Guzik frames the widow's oil and the Shunammite's persistence as models of active faith. Chuck Smith on v.27 stresses that prophetic gifts are from God and can be withheld — a corrective to those who might treat prophecy as an inherent personal power.

- **Lutheran (Keil, cited in Ellicott and Pulpit):** Keil treats the miracles soberly, emphasising that the flour and the staff were "material bases for spiritual activity," never magical. He stresses that Elisha predicts rather than performs the multiplication miracle. Keil also suggests an inferiority of Elisha to Elijah based on the gradual nature of the boy's resurrection — a view Ellicott disputes.

- **Anglican (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary):** Detailed historical-grammatical exegesis with attention to geography, Hebrew language, and cultural context. Both commentaries engage with and refute rationalistic attempts to explain away the miracles (e.g., Bähr and Thenius on the loaves). The Pulpit Commentary explicitly states: "The rationalistic attempts which have been made to solve the mystery exhibit a weakness and feebleness that are absolutely puerile."

- **Reformed (Maclaren, cited by Enduring Word):** Maclaren emphasises the humility of Elisha in admitting his ignorance ("The Lord hath hid it from me") and draws a Christological typology from v.34 (Elisha stretching over the dead child as a picture of the incarnation).

---

## Other Views

- **Rationalist/critical views (Bähr, Thenius, cited in Ellicott and Pulpit):** These older critical scholars denied the miraculous element. Bähr argued the hundred men were merely satisfied with small portions (no actual multiplication). Thenius suggested the provisions were adequate for a hundred men without any miracle. Both views are firmly rejected by Ellicott, Keil, and the Pulpit Commentary as contrary to the writer's intent.

- **Catholic/Orthodox readings:** The searches did not return specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this passage from the permitted sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org).

- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible, bibleodyssey.org):** The searches did not return results from these specific sites for this passage.

---

## Summary of Unavailable Material

- Specific Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist/Wesleyan, and modern scholarly readings could not be located within the search and fetch limits.
- Denominational distinctives on this passage are generally minor; the traditional Protestant reading is broadly shared across traditions, with differences more in application than interpretation.
